title: Costs, break-even and depreciation
subtitle: Which costs change with the decision, where revenue overtakes cost, and how an asset’s value is spread over its life.

sections.title: Kinds of cost
sections.body:
Run a small bakery in your mind. The rent is due whether you bake ten loaves or a thousand. The flour, though, depends on how many you bake. That single observation sorts almost every cost you will ever meet. Fixed costs do not change with output (rent, insurance); variable costs do (materials, energy). And separately, direct costs trace to a product, while indirect (overhead) do not.

Now the most important rule in the chapter: a sunk cost is already spent and irrecoverable, so it must be ignored in a forward-looking decision. It hurts, but it is gone. Say you paid Rs 50,000 for a machine that is now worth Rs 20,000 if sold. The Rs 50,000 is sunk; only the Rs 20,000 matters today. Finally, marginal cost is the cost of one more unit, the question every manager asks before saying yes to one more order.

questions.prompt: You paid Rs 50,000 for a machine that is now worth Rs 20,000 if sold. The Rs 50,000 is…

choices.text: A sunk cost — ignore it; compare the future options.
The value to use in the decision.

keynotes: Fixed costs do not change with output (rent, insurance); variable costs do (materials, energy).
Direct costs trace to a product; indirect (overhead) costs do not.
A sunk cost is already spent and irrecoverable and must be ignored in a forward-looking decision.
Marginal cost is the cost of one more unit.

sections.title: Total, average and marginal cost
sections.body:
Put the costs together. Total cost TC = FC + VC. Divide by quantity and you get average cost AC = TC/Q. Here is a lovely pattern: AC falls while marginal cost MC is below it and rises when MC is above it, so MC cuts AC at its minimum, the efficient scale. It is just like a running average of your exam marks: a score below the average pulls it down, one above pulls it up.

Try the numbers. With FC = 120,000 and variable cost Rs 30 per unit, AC at 4,000 units is 30 + 120,000/4,000 = 60. At an output of 6,000, TC = 120,000 + 30 × 6000 = 300,000 and AC = 300,000/6000 = 50. See how average cost fell from 60 to 50? As the figure says, the fixed cost is spread over more units. That is why bigger volumes make things cheaper.

questions.prompt: Average cost keeps falling as output rises because…

choices.text: Variable cost per unit falls to zero.
Fixed cost is spread over more units.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Until marginal cost exceeds average cost.

figures.caption: Figure 3.2.1 — cost by volume
figures.note: Average cost falls because the fixed cost is spread over more units.

keynotes: Total cost TC = FC + VC and average cost AC = TC/Q.
AC falls while MC is below it and rises when MC is above it, so MC cuts AC at its minimum (the efficient scale).
With FC = 120,000 and Rs 30 variable cost per unit, AC is 60 at 4,000 units and 50 at 6,000.
Average cost falls because the fixed cost is spread over more units.

sections.title: Break-even analysis
sections.body:
Every business owner loses sleep over one question: how many must I sell before I stop losing money? That magic number is the break-even point, where revenue (price × quantity) equals total cost.

The formula is friendly: Q* = FC/(p − v), the fixed cost divided by the contribution margin per unit, which is what each sale contributes towards paying the fixed bill. Selling price Rs 50, variable cost Rs 30, FC Rs 120,000: the contribution is 50 − 30 = 20, so Q* = 120,000/20 = 6,000 units. Above it profit is (p − v)(Q − Q*). In the break-even table the profit crosses zero at 6,000 units. And if you cut the fixed costs, do you think the break-even quantity goes up or down?

questions.prompt: Reducing fixed costs makes the break-even quantity…

problems.prompt: FC = Rs 90,000, price Rs 45, variable cost Rs 25. Break-even units, and profit at 6,000 units?

keynotes: Break-even is where revenue equals total cost: Q* = FC/(p − v), fixed cost over the contribution margin per unit.
With price Rs 50, variable cost Rs 30 and FC Rs 120,000, the contribution is 20 and Q* = 6,000 units.
Above break-even, profit is (p − v)(Q − Q*).

sections.title: Depreciation: why and what
sections.body:
A truck does not lose all its value on the day you buy it; it fades a little every year. Accounting captures that fade with depreciation, which allocates the asset’s cost over its life as an expense. A subtle but vital point: depreciation is not a cash outflow, because the cash went out when the asset was bought.

Two terms to know. Book value = cost − accumulated depreciation, and it never drops below the salvage value, so at the end of the asset’s life the book value equals the salvage value. Why does depreciation matter for money at all? Because it is tax-deductible, as you will see in a few pages.

questions.prompt: Book value at the end of the asset’s life equals…

keynotes: Depreciation allocates an asset’s cost over its life as an expense; it is not a cash outflow.
Book value = cost − accumulated depreciation, and never drops below salvage value.
Depreciation matters for money because it is tax-deductible.

sections.title: Straight-line method
sections.body: The simplest way to spread the cost is also the fairest-looking: the same amount every year. Straight-line depreciation is D = (P − S)/N. For P = Rs 100,000, S = Rs 10,000 and N = 5, that is (100,000 − 10,000)/5 = 18,000 per year, and the book value falls by that same step each year. A straight line on the chart, hence the name.

problems.prompt: A Rs 240,000 machine has a 6-year life and Rs 30,000 salvage. Annual straight-line depreciation and book value after year 4?

keynotes: Straight-line depreciation charges D = (P − S)/N, the same every year.
With P = Rs 100,000, S = Rs 10,000 and N = 5, D is 18,000 per year.
Book value falls by the same step each year.

sections.title: Declining-balance and MACRS
sections.body:
Is a new car worth the same drop in its first year as in its tenth? Of course not; it loses most of its value early. Declining-balance methods copy that reality. Double declining balance takes a fixed fraction 2/N of the remaining book value each year, ignoring salvage until the end and never going below it, so the deductions are bigger early.

Same asset as before: the rate is 2/N = 2/5 = 40 %. Year 1 on Rs 100,000 gives 40,000 and leaves a book value of 60,000. Year 2 is 40 % of 60,000 = 24,000. Then year 3 14,400, year 4 8,640, year 5 2,960. Compare with straight-line’s flat 18,000, and you can see the front-loading! MACRS (used for tax in the USA) assigns standard percentage tables per asset class. Why would a firm prefer accelerated depreciation? Think about when the tax savings arrive.

worked.why: Depreciation then = 40,000; book value 60,000. Year 2 = 40 % of 60,000 = 24,000.

questions.prompt: Why do firms like accelerated depreciation?

choices.text: Bigger early tax deductions, so tax is deferred.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Money now is worth more than later.

keynotes: Double declining balance takes 2/N of the remaining book value each year, never going below salvage.
MACRS, used for tax in the USA, assigns standard percentage tables per asset class.
Deductions come early, so tax savings arrive sooner.

sections.title: Income taxes in decisions
sections.body:
Governments take a bite of profit, so a real decision has to be made after tax. Taxable income = revenue − operating cost − depreciation, and Tax = rate × taxable income. The after-tax cash flow = (revenue − cost) − tax.

Notice the hidden gift: depreciation lowers taxable income, creating a tax shield of rate × D each year. Work an example. Revenue 80,000, cash costs 30,000, depreciation 18,000, tax rate 30 %. Taxable income = 32,000, tax = 9,600, and after-tax cash flow = 50,000 − 9,600 = 40,400. With D = 18,000 and 30 % tax, the shield is 5,400. Depreciation costs no cash, yet it saves you money.

worked.why: Revenue 80,000, cash costs 30,000, depreciation 18,000, tax rate 30 %.

questions.prompt: The tax shield from depreciation equals…

problems.prompt: Depreciation is Rs 25,000 a year and the tax rate 35 %. Annual tax shield?

keynotes: Taxable income = revenue − operating cost − depreciation, and tax = rate × taxable income.
After-tax cash flow = (revenue − cost) − tax.
Depreciation creates a tax shield of rate × D each year.
Revenue 80,000, costs 30,000, depreciation 18,000 and 30 % tax give taxable income 32,000, tax 9,600 and after-tax cash flow 40,400.
